title: Why Are There Balls on Power Lines?

scenes.text: Drive near an airport or across a big river valley and you may see giant colored balls hanging on power lines, orange, white and yellow, high above the ground. They look like toys someone threw up there. They are not. Each one may be saving a pilot's life. Today, eleven parts of a high voltage power line, and why each one exists, starting with those balls.
scenes.caption: WHY ARE THERE BALLS UP THERE?

scenes.text: Power lines carry electricity from power plants to cities, sometimes over hundreds of kilometers, at hundreds of thousands of volts. They cross mountains, rivers and forests. They are hit by wind, ice, lightning and birds. And almost nothing on them is decoration. Every strange object you see on a power line is there to solve a problem.
scenes.caption: NOTHING IS DECORATION

scenes.text: As always, every fact comes from a named source, power companies, aviation authorities, and official investigation reports, all listed in the description. Let's start with the balls.
scenes.caption: WHY DOES THIS EXIST?

scenes.text: Why are there big colored balls on some power lines? Because pilots cannot see the wires. A thin cable stretched across a valley is almost invisible from the air, even in good weather. Low flying aircraft, like helicopters, crop dusters and small planes, have crashed into power lines they never saw. The balls make the wires visible from far away.
scenes.caption: WHY ARE THERE BALLS ON POWER LINES?
scenes.short: Why Are There Balls on Power Lines?

scenes.text: They are called aerial marker balls, and aviation rules say where they must go. Usually near airports, across rivers and canyons, and on very high spans. In the United States, they can be up to about ninety centimeters across, in orange, white or yellow, and the colors alternate along the line so they stand out against the sky and the ground.
scenes.caption: ORANGE, WHITE, YELLOW

scenes.text: The balls are hollow, made of light plastic or fiberglass, so they add little weight to the line. They are clamped on by line workers, often from a helicopter. A few kilograms of plastic make a deadly cable impossible to miss.
scenes.caption: HOLLOW BUT LIFE SAVING

scenes.text: Why do power lines have small dumbbell shaped weights hanging near the towers? They are Stockbridge dampers, invented in the nineteen twenties by an engineer named George Stockbridge. They stop the wires from vibrating themselves to death. A steady breeze blowing across a cable sheds tiny swirls of air, which make the cable vibrate up and down very fast, with small movements.
scenes.caption: WHY ARE THERE DUMBBELLS ON THESE WIRES?
scenes.short: Why Do Power Lines Have Little Dumbbells on Them?
scenes.file: File:Stockbridge damper on 150kV power line Maarheeze - Eindhoven Oost.jpg

scenes.text: This is called aeolian vibration, after the Greek god of the wind. It is too small to see easily, but it never stops. Over months and years, the bending at the clamps tires the metal strands, and they can break one by one. A broken conductor can drop a live wire to the ground.
scenes.caption: VIBRATING TO DEATH

scenes.text: The two weights hang on a short piece of flexible steel cable. When the wire vibrates, the weights swing and flex that cable, turning the vibration energy into a little heat. It is one of the simplest and most successful inventions in power engineering, and it is still used all over the world.
scenes.caption: SIMPLE AND STILL USED

scenes.text: Why do the biggest power lines use groups of two, three or four wires, held apart by metal frames? Because one thick wire would waste energy into the air. At very high voltages, the electric field around a single wire is so strong that it rips electrons off the air molecules. That is called corona discharge. It wastes power, makes noise, and causes radio interference.
scenes.caption: WHY ARE THESE WIRES IN BUNDLES?
scenes.short: Why Do Power Lines Use Bundles of Wires?
scenes.file: File:Spacer Electric Line Chandigre West Garo Oct24 A7CR 03547.jpg

scenes.text: Splitting each phase into a bundle of smaller wires spreads the electric field out, like making the wire act thicker without the weight. The bundle also carries more current. The metal frames, called spacers, keep the wires at the right distance, so they do not slap together in the wind or when a short circuit pulls them toward each other.
scenes.caption: ACTING THICKER

scenes.text: On a damp day, you can sometimes hear a crackling buzz under high voltage lines. That is corona, the air itself conducting a tiny bit. The bundles and spacers keep it small. Without them, the buzz would be much louder and the losses much higher.
scenes.caption: THE BUZZ

scenes.text: Why do power line insulators look like stacks of glass or ceramic plates? Because they must keep hundreds of thousands of volts away from the steel tower. Each disc can hold back a certain voltage, so the higher the voltage of the line, the more discs in the string. You can roughly guess a line's voltage by counting them.
scenes.caption: WHY DO THESE INSULATORS LOOK LIKE PLATES?
scenes.short: Why Do Power Line Insulators Look Like Stacks of Plates?

scenes.text: The wavy shape is important. Dirt, salt and rain can form a wet path on the surface, and electricity can creep along it. The ridges under each disc make the path along the surface much longer, and keep part of it dry in the rain, so the current cannot sneak across.
scenes.caption: A LONGER PATH

scenes.text: Glass discs have a clever safety feature. If one is damaged by a bullet or a power surge, it shatters completely and visibly, while the metal parts keep holding the line. Inspectors flying by can see the missing disc right away. Many new lines use long rubber polymer insulators, which are lighter and resist vandalism better.
scenes.caption: GLASS THAT SHATTERS ON PURPOSE

scenes.text: Why do some insulators have shiny metal rings around their ends? They are corona rings, also called grading rings. At the end of an insulator, the electric field gets concentrated on sharp edges and small metal parts. That concentrated field causes corona discharge, which slowly damages the insulator and wastes energy.
scenes.caption: WHY ARE THERE RINGS ON THESE INSULATORS?
scenes.chapter: 5. The metal rings at the ends
scenes.short: Why Do High Voltage Lines Have Metal Rings?

scenes.text: A smooth, round ring spreads the field out over a larger surface, the same way the bundles do for the wires. On polymer insulators, this protects the rubber, which can be burned by constant tiny discharges. On the highest voltage lines, you will see rings at both ends of every insulator.
scenes.caption: SPREADING THE FIELD

scenes.text: It is a rule you see all over high voltage equipment. Sharp points are bad, smooth curves are good. That is why substations are full of round tubes, domes and rings. Electricity at these voltages leaks from anything pointy.
scenes.caption: NO SHARP POINTS

scenes.text: Why do many power towers have one or two thin wires running along their very tops, above the main wires? They are shield wires, or ground wires. They are connected to the steel towers and to the earth, and they catch lightning. A strike on the shield wire flows down the towers into the ground instead of hitting the live wires below.
scenes.caption: WHY IS THERE A WIRE ABOVE THE OTHERS?
scenes.chapter: 6. The wire on the very top
scenes.short: Why Is There an Extra Wire on Top of Power Towers?

scenes.text: Without them, a lightning strike on a power wire would send a huge surge along the line, damaging equipment and tripping the power off. The shield wires create a kind of protective tent above the conductors, like an umbrella against lightning.
scenes.caption: AN UMBRELLA FOR LIGHTNING

scenes.text: Many modern shield wires have a hidden second job. Inside, they carry optical fibers. Power companies use them to send control signals, and some rent the extra fibers to telecom companies. A wire meant to catch lightning also carries internet traffic.
scenes.caption: INTERNET INSIDE

scenes.text: Why do some power lines have small spirals or flapping tags clipped on them? They are bird diverters. Large birds, like cranes, swans, storks and bustards, often cannot see thin wires until it is too late, especially in fog or at dusk. Collisions with power lines kill huge numbers of birds every year.
scenes.caption: WHY ARE THERE SPIRALS ON THIS WIRE?
scenes.short: Why Do Power Lines Have Spirals for Birds?
scenes.file: File:Power line bird flight diverter - geograph.org.uk - 6065689.jpg

scenes.text: The diverters make the wires thicker and more visible, and some flap, glow or reflect light. Studies have found that marking lines can greatly reduce bird collisions, often cutting them by half or more, depending on the species and the place.
scenes.caption: HALF THE COLLISIONS

scenes.text: Power companies also design towers so that birds landing on them cannot touch two wires at once, which would electrocute them. Some even build nest platforms on towers for storks and ospreys, giving them a safe place away from the live wires.
scenes.caption: SAFE NESTS

scenes.text: Why do many power towers have barbed wire or spiked panels on their legs, a few meters above the ground? Because people climb them. Children, thrill seekers and thieves have climbed towers, and some have been killed. You do not have to touch a high voltage wire to be electrocuted. At these voltages, the current can jump through the air if you get close.
scenes.caption: WHY DO THESE TOWERS HAVE BARBED WIRE?
scenes.chapter: 8. The barbed panels on the legs
scenes.short: Why Do Power Towers Have Barbed Wire on Their Legs?
scenes.file: File:Transmission towers at sunset in East Texas.jpg

scenes.text: The anti climbing devices make the first few meters very hard to climb, and danger signs warn of death. Line workers who need to go up use special access points and switch off or work with strict safety distances.
scenes.caption: DANGER OF DEATH

scenes.text: Even kites and drones are dangerous near power lines. A wet kite string can conduct electricity, and a drone touching a wire can short it out. The safest rule is the simple one. Stay well away from anything attached to a power line.
scenes.caption: STAY AWAY

scenes.text: How can a line worker touch a power line carrying hundreds of thousands of volts and survive? Because current only flows when there is a difference in voltage. Workers on a platform hanging from a helicopter wear suits woven with metal threads. They first touch the wire with a metal wand, so that they, the suit and the helicopter rise to the same voltage as the line.
scenes.caption: WHY IS THIS MAN TOUCHING A LIVE WIRE?
scenes.chapter: 9. The man on the live wire
scenes.short: Why Can This Man Touch a Live Power Line?
scenes.file: File:New overhead transmission line construction - Flickr - brewbooks.jpg

scenes.text: Once they are at the same voltage, no current flows through their bodies, the same reason birds can sit on a single wire. The metal suit acts like a Faraday cage, keeping the electric field around them. They can then repair spacers, replace insulators or fix damaged strands, without switching off the power to a whole region.
scenes.caption: SAME VOLTAGE, NO CURRENT

scenes.text: The dangerous moment is the connection, when a bright arc jumps between the wand and the wire. After that, the worker can sit on the line as if it were a bench. It is one of the most extreme jobs in the world, and it only works because the physics is exactly right.
scenes.caption: SITTING ON THE LINE

scenes.text: Why do power lines hang in a curve instead of being pulled tight? Because a perfectly tight wire would need enormous force, and it would snap when it shrank in the cold. So lines are hung with a planned sag. But that sag changes. When a line carries a lot of current, it heats up, the metal expands, and the wire droops lower.
scenes.caption: WHY DO POWER LINES SAG?
scenes.short: Why Do Power Lines Sag More on Hot Days?
scenes.file: File:Wire marker signals danger for helicopters 20090320 001.JPG

scenes.text: On the fourteenth of August two thousand three, in Ohio, hot heavily loaded lines sagged into trees that had not been trimmed. They shorted out one after another. Alarm software had failed, so operators did not see what was happening. The failure spread into the largest blackout in North American history, cutting power to about fifty million people.
scenes.caption: THE 2003 BLACKOUT

scenes.text: That is why power companies keep wide clear strips under their lines, cutting trees and bushes. The space under a power line is not empty by accident. It is the room the wire needs on its hottest day.
scenes.caption: ROOM TO SAG

scenes.text: Why do power lines run at such dangerous voltages, hundreds of thousands of volts? Because it saves energy. The power lost in a wire depends on the current squared. If you raise the voltage ten times, you can send the same power with a tenth of the current, and the losses drop to about a hundredth.
scenes.caption: WHY DOES POWER TRAVEL AT SUCH HIGH VOLTAGE?
scenes.short: Why Does Electricity Travel at Such High Voltage?

scenes.text: That is why electricity leaves the power plant through a transformer that raises the voltage, travels across the country on tall towers, and is then stepped down again in substations near the city, and once more on the pole outside your house. The giant towers exist because the voltage needs big distances from the ground and between the wires.
scenes.caption: UP, ACROSS, DOWN

scenes.text: Most lines carry three wires, or three bundles, because the grid uses three phase power, three currents that rise and fall one after the other. It is the most efficient way to move large amounts of power, and it is why many towers have their wires in groups of three.
scenes.caption: GROUPS OF THREE

scenes.text: So here are the eleven. Colored balls for pilots, and little dumbbells that stop the vibration. Bundles of wires with spacers, insulators like stacks of plates, and metal rings that spread the field. A wire on top that catches lightning, spirals for birds, barbed wire against climbers, a man on a live wire, a sag that caused a blackout, and voltages high enough to save the energy.
scenes.caption: 11 PARTS. 500,000 VOLTS.

scenes.text: Next time you drive under a power line, look up, and you will know what everything up there is for. If you want more machines and structures explained part by part, subscribe to Machine Reverse. And tell us in the comments what you want us to take apart next.
scenes.caption: SUBSCRIBE: MACHINE REVERSE
